title: Choosing, locating, and asking about things

grammarPoints.title: これ・それ・あれ・どれ
grammarPoints.meaning: These stand alone as noun-like words for this one, that one near the listener, that one away from both speakers, and which one.
grammarPoints.formation: これ／それ／あれ + は + noun predicate; どれ appears in a question such as どれですか or どれが…ですか.
notes: Choose the demonstrative by distance from speaker and listener, not by English this/that alone.
Avoid pointing to a nearby person in earshot with the これ/それ/あれ series; a name or title is more natural.
どれ is a question word; when it is the grammatical subject in ‘which one is X?’, use が rather than は.
いくらですか asks the price. To answer, put a yen amount before です.

schemas.context: Point to a thing {demonstrative:distance}.
schemas.omission: A clear topic may be omitted in conversation; the model keeps it explicit.
restrictions: Choose これ, それ or あれ using the distance. The distance belongs to the selected demonstrative, so it cannot contradict it.

schemas.context: Several things of the same type are visible. Ask which belongs to the named person.
schemas.omission: A clear topic may be omitted in conversation; the model keeps it explicit.
restrictions: Use が with question subject どれ, as introduced in this section’s note; どれは is not a question-subject pattern.

schemas.context: You are shopping. Point to an item {demonstrative:distance}.
schemas.omission: A clear topic may be omitted in conversation; the model keeps it explicit.
restrictions: いくら asks price. The demonstrative stands alone without an additional noun.

grammarPoints.title: この・その・あの・どの + noun
grammarPoints.meaning: Use this demonstrative series directly before a noun to identify which person or thing is meant.
grammarPoints.formation: この／その／あの／どの + noun. Unlike これ and its series, these forms cannot stand alone.
notes: この is near the speaker, その near the listener, あの away from both, and どの asks which one.
The noun must immediately follow; do not add は directly after この／その／あの.
These can refer to people, unlike the standalone これ/それ/あれ forms in ordinary conversation.

examples.english: That item near you is a watch.
examples.kana: そのしなものはとけいです。

examples.japanese: どの学生がカナダ人ですか。
examples.kana: どのがくせいがカナダじんですか。

schemas.context: State the price of an item {determiner:distance}.
schemas.omission: A clear topic may be omitted in conversation; the model keeps it explicit.
restrictions: Keep the noun immediately after この, その or あの. The prices are plausible shop amounts for every item in the pool.

schemas.context: Several items of this type are visible. Ask which belongs to the named person.
schemas.omission: A clear topic may be omitted in conversation; the model keeps it explicit.
restrictions: どの modifies the noun. Use が for the unknown subject and retain the owned noun in this beginner pattern.

schemas.context: Identify the nationality of someone {determiner:distance}.
schemas.omission: A clear topic may be omitted in conversation; the model keeps it explicit.
restrictions: Unlike standalone これ, この + a person noun can politely identify a person. The predicate is a nationality, avoiding contradictory roles.

schemas.context: Ask the price of an item {determiner:distance}.
schemas.omission: A clear topic may be omitted in conversation; the model keeps it explicit.
restrictions: The item noun must follow the この-series determiner.

grammarPoints.title: ここ・そこ・あそこ・どこ
grammarPoints.meaning: Use these words to refer to places: here near the speaker, there near the listener, over there, or where.
grammarPoints.formation: A question uses [place/topic] は どこですか; an answer can use ここ／そこ／あそこ + です.
notes: The こ・そ・あ distance pattern matches the demonstratives from the previous section.

examples.kana: としょかんはどこですか。

examples.english: The post office is over there.
examples.kana: ゆうびんきょくはあそこです。

schemas.instruction: Ask where the place is in Japanese.
schemas.context: You are politely asking someone for directions.
schemas.omission: The place topic can be omitted when already obvious.
restrictions: Use a place noun in the topic slot.

schemas.context: The place is {location:distance}. Point it out to the listener.
schemas.omission: A clear topic may be omitted in conversation; the model keeps it explicit.
restrictions: Use only ここ, そこ or あそこ as a statement predicate; どこ belongs in a question.

grammarPoints.title: だれの + noun
grammarPoints.meaning: Ask who owns or is associated with an item by placing だれの before its noun.
grammarPoints.formation: だれの + noun; answer with owner + の + noun.
notes: This extends the noun-linking particle の from Lesson 1; the question word だれ means who.

examples.kana: これはだれのかさですか。

examples.japanese: ユイさんのノートです。
examples.kana: ユイさんのノートです。

schemas.context: You found an item and are politely asking about its owner.
schemas.omission: The item is retained because it is the noun modified by だれの.
restrictions: Keep だれの immediately before the owned noun.

schemas.instruction: Answer with the owner's name in Japanese.
schemas.context: You are identifying the person who owns an item.
schemas.omission: The topic is omitted because it is a short answer; the item may be omitted if already identified.
restrictions: The owner must be a person and the head noun an owned item.

grammarPoints.title: も for ‘also’
grammarPoints.meaning: も marks a newly mentioned person or thing as sharing an attribute already established for another item.
grammarPoints.formation: Replace the earlier topic marker は with も on the parallel item: A は X です。B も X です。
notes: Put も directly after the parallel item, not at the end of the sentence.
The meaning depends on an earlier matching item or shared property; it is not a general marker for two unrelated facts.
This lesson models も in topic position. Other particle combinations are introduced later.

examples.english: Aoi is a student. Ken is a student too.
examples.japanese: アオイさんは学生です。ケンさんも学生です。
examples.kana: アオイさんはがくせいです。ケンさんもがくせいです。

schemas.instruction: Translate the second sentence into Japanese.
schemas.context: You have already said that {first-person} is {identity}. Now add that {second-person} shares that fact.
schemas.omission: The previously mentioned person is in the context; the new parallel topic remains explicit.
restrictions: Both people must plausibly share the same identity; do not use も to express two different attributes of one person.

grammarPoints.title: Negative noun sentences
grammarPoints.meaning: Negate a noun predicate politely to say that the topic is not a member of the stated category.
grammarPoints.formation: Noun + じゃないです. More conservative speech uses じゃありません; formal writing commonly uses ではありません.
notes: Keep the noun before the negative expression; じゃないです does not stand alone as ‘no’.
じゃ is a contraction of では. Match the chosen form to the context's politeness level.
This pattern negates noun predicates only. Adjectives use their own conjugation patterns, taught later.

examples.japanese: リンさんは先生じゃないです。
examples.kana: リンさんはせんせいじゃないです。

examples.japanese: そこは図書館ではありません。
examples.kana: そこはとしょかんではありません。

schemas.instruction: Write this polite negative sentence in Japanese.
schemas.context: You are correcting a mistaken assumption about {person}.
schemas.omission: The topic may be omitted if clear, but keep it when correcting a specific assumption.
restrictions: Use a noun predicate here. Do not attach じゃないです directly to an い-adjective; adjective patterns arrive in Lesson 5.

schemas.context: Someone has asked whether you have this identity. Correct them politely.
schemas.omission: The question establishes the speaker as topic, so 私は is naturally omitted.
restrictions: Retain the identity noun; いいえ、じゃないです alone is incomplete.

grammarPoints.title: Sentence-final ね and よ
grammarPoints.meaning: Add ね when inviting confirmation or agreement; use よ to assert or supply information with confidence to the listener.
grammarPoints.formation: Polite statement + ね or よ.
notes: ね and よ express different speaker-listener stances; they are not interchangeable decoration.
Either can follow a negative noun sentence as well as an affirmative one.

examples.japanese: これはユイさんのノートですね。
examples.kana: これはユイさんのノートですね。

examples.english: That is not a wallet, you know.
examples.japanese: あれは財布じゃないですよ。
examples.kana: あれはさいふじゃないですよ。

schemas.context: You believe this fact and invite the listener to confirm it.
schemas.omission: A clear topic may be omitted in conversation; the model keeps it explicit.
restrictions: Use ね to seek agreement.

schemas.context: Correct a mistaken assumption confidently; you already know the answer.
schemas.omission: A clear topic may be omitted in conversation; the model keeps it explicit.
restrictions: Use よ to supply information, not to ask for confirmation.

schemas.context: The listener is unsure about this person. Tell them the fact confidently.
schemas.omission: A clear topic may be omitted in conversation; the model keeps it explicit.
restrictions: Use よ for new or correcting information.

schemas.context: You think the negative fact is true and want confirmation.
schemas.omission: A clear topic may be omitted in conversation; the model keeps it explicit.
restrictions: ね can follow a negative predicate; retain the negative copula.

grammarPoints.title: Requesting and offering things
grammarPoints.meaning: Use をください to ask for a concrete thing. をお願いします is a polite request often heard when ordering, and をどうぞ offers an item to someone.
grammarPoints.formation: Item を ください／お願いします／どうぞ.
notes: These are useful set request patterns here; general verb-object sentences arrive in Lesson 3.
ください requests a concrete object. お願いします also works for services, but this practice stays with tangible items.
In an obvious handover, を or the whole item phrase may be omitted.

examples.english: Here is some water for you.

schemas.context: Politely request a concrete item at a counter.
schemas.omission: A clear topic may be omitted in conversation; the model keeps it explicit.
restrictions: Use a tangible thing; do not substitute an action or attach a verb here.

schemas.context: Place a polite café order.
schemas.omission: A clear topic may be omitted in conversation; the model keeps it explicit.
restrictions: This schema uses a food or drink noun and the set expression お願いします.

schemas.context: Hand the requested item to the listener.
schemas.omission: A clear topic may be omitted in conversation; the model keeps it explicit.
restrictions: どうぞ offers the item; ください would request it instead.
